chapter: Starting out in New York and Chicago
title: Swingland run, the Chicago union five-day week, Grand Terrace rivals
summary: Swingland ran seven nights a week for three or four years on WBBM until bassist Harry Grey, later local president, won a five-day week. Ed Fox's Grand Terrace had Earl Hines and Fletcher; Lawrence Welk preceded them on air.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: About how many years were you there? Do you recall? Or how long?
At Swingland? I would say, at this particular job, we stayed on it for three to four years, and that's a career.
You bet. Was that six nights a week, or --
This was seven nights a week.

Until this union started in Chicago, and then we went down to five. My -- of course, my bass player at that time was a guy named Harry Grey who later became the President of the Musicians' Local in Chicago. There was two locals at that time -- local 10 and our local in Chicago. And Harry Grey was the President -- he didn't want to run, we had to make him run for office. And he won by a landslide. So, he was quite a guy. So he was the one that got us a five-day week deal with seven-day pay, you know.

And this was during the great days of the Grand Terrace when they were broadcasting. Ed Fox was the name of the guy that owned the Grand Terrace where Fletcher played after Earl Hines. In fact, he had a contract on Earl

and Fletcher. Those were his two bands, and I was in Swingland, and I used to battle these guys, and Lawrence Welk was across town playing his squeeze box with his seven piece group, and he used to come on a half hour before us on WBBM. I wish I had carried his squeeze box (unintelligible) because he laughs all the way to the bank.
You bet. About what year was this?
